title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent-Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and an automated single-repair step—reduces unsafe network changes relative to LLM-only generation. Following a preregistered paired design (N=500 intents run under both pipelines), we used gpt-5-mini for generation and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) as the adjudicating oracle. The GVR condition produced 500/500 safe accepted changes versus 496/500 for LLM-only (paired difference = 0.008; 95% bootstrap CI [0.002, 0.016]; exact McNemar two-sided p = 0.125; per-test alpha=0.025, Bonferroni family alpha=0.05). The difference is numerically favorable to GVR but not significant at the preregistered threshold. Exploratory diagnostics show only 4 repair calls were invoked (total model calls = 504; mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 1.008; median repair iterations under GVR = 0). We report the completed preregistered artifacts, describe practical failure modes, and discuss limitations—principally synthetic tasks, single-model scope, and verifier modeling assumptions—and recommend multi-model, multi-verifier follow-ups before production adoption.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network changes promises operational efficiency but risks outages and policy violations when generated changes are incorrect or unsafe. Large language models (LLMs) can translate high-level intent to device commands, yet hallucination and sequence errors undermine trust for NetOps automation. Deterministic configuration verifiers can detect many correctness violations before deployment, suggesting a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline as an operational safeguard. We asked: Does GVR (LLM + deterministic verifier + single automated repair opportunity) reduce unsafe changes compared with LLM-only generation? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired experiment over N=500 intents stratified by templateability and topology profiles, (2) an autonomous execution producing the full raw-artifact bundle and analyses, and (3) a transparent quantitative result set and failure-mode diagnostics grounded in the archived execution.
sections.related_work: Prior literature documents extensive interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks including intent-to-configuration translation, AIOps/fault diagnosis, and multi-agent management frameworks. Surveys and system papers observe hallucination and reliability concerns that motivate verifier-augmented architectures; parallel work proposes tool-augmented agents and verification systems (e.g., distributed verifiers) to improve safety. Security studies highlight prompt-injection and adversarial risks to LLM pipelines, underscoring the need for guarded generation and input sanitation. At the same time, formal and deterministic verifiers (and their distributed scalings) have matured for many reachability and policy checks, but prior work lacks systematic, preregistered paired trials comparing end-to-end GVR pipelines with plain LLM generation on standardized NetOps change workloads. This study was designed to address that gap within the constrained experimental scope.
sections.methodology: Design and preregistration: We preregistered study 'study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29' before observing outcomes. The primary research question and confirmatory hypotheses were pre-specified; the primary estimand was the paired success-rate difference (GVR minus LLM-only). Sampling: 500 distinct intents (paired), stratified 60% templateable/40% complex across 10 synthetic topology profiles. Model and pipelines: generation used gpt-5-mini; the GVR (guarded) condition executed generation, deterministic verification (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and allowed one automated repair attempt (maximum repair calls per task = 1) when the verifier failed. Baseline (LLM-only) used shared initial generation without automated repair; a templated-automation comparator was preregistered but not executed. Execution constraints: maximum model calls = 1000; completed episodes = 1000 (500 pairs). Primary analysis: paired binary outcomes (success = final accepted change passes primary verifier). Statistical tests: exact paired-proportion test (McNemar exact where applicable) with 95% bootstrap percentile CIs using 10,000 resamples stratified by task_id. Multiplicity: two confirmatory tests were preregistered; Bonferroni correction applied (family alpha = 0.05 => per-test alpha = 0.025). Missingness and technical failures: preregistered rules applied (complete-pair primary analysis; sensitivity treating missing as unsafe also pre-specified). All prompts, model outputs, verifier logs, task manifests, and hashes are archived in the execution bundle referenced in the Evidence section.
sections.results: Execution summary: planned episodes = 1000; completed = 1000; total model calls used = 504 (shared_initial_generation stage_count = 500; repair stage_count = 4). Primary confirmatory outcome (paired analysis over 500 complete pairs): guarded successes = 500/500 (1.000); baseline successes = 496/500 (0.992). Paired contingency (guarded, baseline): n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Estimated paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.008 (0.8 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 0.125. Paired bootstrap 95% CI for the difference = [0.002, 0.016] (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples). Interpretation against preregistered threshold: the observed improvement favors GVR numerically, but the effect does not reach the preregistered per-test significance level (α = 0.025). Confirmatory secondary comparison versus templated automation was not executed (templated arm absent) and is reported as unexecuted. Exploratory diagnostics: only 4 repair calls were invoked across 500 guarded tasks (median repair iterations under GVR = 0), total model-call overhead per accepted change ≈ 1.008. Contamination and missingness checks: complete-pair count = 500; no provider-call failures recorded; verifier disagreement audit flagged zero primary/secondary inconsistencies under the primary-adjudicator workflow. All primary numbers and artifacts reconcile deterministically with the archived manifests.
sections.discussion: The experiment demonstrates that a deterministic-verifier–backed GVR pipeline can eliminate the small number of unsafe changes observed under LLM-only generation in this synthetic workload (0 vs 4 unsafe cases). However, the absolute improvement (0.8 percentage points) is small and not statistically significant at the preregistered corrected alpha. Practical implications: in contexts where even rare unsafe changes are unacceptable, integrating a verifier into an LLM-driven pipeline may provide strong operational benefit with modest model-call overhead as observed here. Caveats: (1) task realism—this study used synthetic topologies and anonymized device-agnostic CLIs; (2) single-model scope—results reflect gpt-5-mini behavior and may differ for other LLMs; (3) verifier modeling—the deterministic validator encodes a specific subset of operational correctness checks (its coverage defines observed safety), so GVR benefits scale with verifier completeness; (4) templated automation comparison was not executed and remains an open confirmatory test. Future work should broaden model and verifier diversity, evaluate adversarial robustness of the pipeline against NetOps-tailored inputs, and measure human-in-the-loop latency/cost trade-offs in near-production settings.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment with N=500 intents, a generate–verify–repair pipeline using gpt-5-mini plus a deterministic network verifier produced numerically fewer unsafe changes than LLM-only generation (500 vs 496 safe outcomes). The observed 0.8 percentage-point paired improvement favored GVR but did not meet the preregistered significance threshold after multiplicity correction (p = 0.125; 95% CI [0.002, 0.016]). The GVR approach incurred negligible model-call overhead in this run (mean calls ≈ 1.008 per accepted change) and invoked repairs rarely. These results support the operational promise of verifier-augmented LLM pipelines while underscoring the need for wider replication (multiple models, richer task corpora, and more comprehensive verifiers) before concluding production readiness. All preregistered artifacts, raw outputs, verifier traces, and analysis files are archived with the execution manifest for reproducibility and inspection.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor-specific CLIs, and live telemetry is untested.
Single-generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi-model generality is not established.
Safety signal limited to the deterministic validator's coverage (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); verifier blind spots may mask other operational risks.
The templated-automation comparator, preregistered as a confirmatory arm, was not executed and thus the GVR vs templated confirmatory hypothesis is untested.
Adversarial robustness and prompt-injection resilience for NetOps-formatted malicious inputs were not evaluated and remain future work.
